sections.overview: The European hedgehog is a ground-dwelling insectivore native to much of Europe; people introduced it to New Zealand. Short legs and a pointed snout suit foraging in low cover. Mostly active after dark, it hibernates when cold weather reduces prey. Its spiny back protects it when curled. The IUCN’s 2024 assessment classifies it Near Threatened.
sections.identification: The adult has a pointed snout, small eyes and short limbs. Brown-and-cream keratin spines cover its crown and back; face, limbs and belly bear fur. A broad muscle sheet under the skin draws head and limbs inward while smaller muscles raise the spines, enclosing vulnerable surfaces in a defensive ball. The Mammal Society gives a head-and-body length of 15–30 cm, a 1–2 cm tail and a mass of up to 2 kg; the range varies with age. The source does not report a reliable male–female size difference or a body-width measure.
sections.habitat: The species uses pasture margins, hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges, parks and gardens. It benefits where cover, prey and nesting material occur together; large exposed fields offer fewer refuges. By day it rests in nests and makes a sturdier winter shelter from dry leaves, supported by nearby vegetation or other objects. The nest insulates and protects it during hibernation. Use of gardens and farmland depends on local cover and food, so habitat use varies among populations.
sections.diet: Food consists mainly of ground invertebrates: slugs, snails, earthworms, beetles and other insects. DNA analysis of faeces from 193 hedgehogs admitted to rescue centres in northern Belgium detected slugs and snails in 92% of samples, earthworms and beetles in 54% each. These frequencies describe that sample, not a universal diet. The study also detected occasional vertebrate prey and human-provided foods. The hedgehog is opportunistic, but invertebrates remain its characteristic natural food.
sections.behavior: Radio-tracking in Switzerland found a mostly nocturnal rhythm, with strong activity early in the night and marked variation among individuals. Smell and hearing help locate prey; the mobile snout probes litter and soil. Adults generally forage alone and do not defend fixed territories. Hibernation lowers body temperature and metabolism, conserving energy during winter food shortages. Animals may arouse and change nests; timing and duration vary with weather, region and body condition.
sections.reproduction: Breeding begins as activity resumes after winter. A male may follow and circle a female before mating; the pair does not remain together and he provides no routine care. After about five weeks of gestation, the female gives birth in a sheltered nest, usually to three to six young; a second litter is possible. Newborns are blind, and their first spines emerge from beneath swollen skin soon after birth. The mother nurses the litter; young become mobile and independent over the following weeks.
sections.ecology: Hedgehogs eat soil and litter invertebrates and are prey for badgers, foxes and large owls; spines deter some predators but do not ensure safety. Their movements connect feeding and nesting areas, and hedgerows can guide travel. Radio-tracking in two English urban sites found roads and verges little used and documented crossings. Roads can therefore kill hedgehogs and impede movement, depending on traffic and landscape. Ticks and fleas also use them as hosts.
sections.conservation: The IUCN’s 2024 publication assigns Near Threatened (NT) globally and in the EU27, from an assessment dated 18 February 2023; the trend is decreasing. Declines in over half of range countries and reductions near or above 30% per decade across extensive areas informed the category. This replaces the 2016 and 2008 global Least Concern assessments. Monitoring remains uneven, so regional populations may differ.
